To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the current legal rules are not efficient; (b) the legal rules are unlikely to have any effect on the efficiency of the market; and (c) the legal rules do not enhance the efficiency of corporate governance.

(i) the current rules are not efficient in the sense that they do not maximize the value of the firm; (ii) the current rules do not maximize the welfare of shareholders; (iii) the current rules maximize the welfare of debtholders; (iv) the current rules may be efficient in the sense of maximizing the welfare of society as a whole, but this is not necessarily so; (v) there are no efficient rules for the raising and maintenance by firms of share capital.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether there is a case for the existence of a set of rules which govern the way in which companies raise and maintain share capital.
the economic case for a number of rules of company law, in particular the rules which regulate the raising of share capital and the maintenance of capital by companies.
the question of whether the current rules of company law, which regulate the raising of share capital by public companies, are economically efficient.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current rules should be abolished and the market should be left to determine the rules which govern the raising of share capital by public companies.
the rules are not efficient, but that they do not have any significant impact on the efficiency of the market.
the current rules should be abolished, and the raising and maintaining of share capital left to market forces.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rules which regulate share capital are unlikely to enhance efficiency in the markets which they are intended to regulate.
there is no economic case for rules which regulate the raising of share capital.
we have found no evidence of a significant economic case for the rules in the Companies Act.

the current rules do not enhance the efficiency of markets in which they operate and are unlikely to do so.
